articles.title: New audit in Walz's backyard exposes massive fraud risk tied to post-George Floyd activism
articles.summary: A Minneapolis audit reveals weak oversight of $36 million in violence prevention contracts tied to programs launched after George Floyd's death.
articles.body: As Minnesota’s massive fraud problems continue to gain nationwide attention, an audit is now sounding the alarm about potential fraud in a new area in the state related to contracts doled out by the city of Minneapolis in response to the death of George Floyd. More than 100 contracts were handed out to community groups as alternatives to policing in 2020 and the lax oversight of those contracts, according to a Minnesota Star Tribune report, was found by an audit to be susceptible to fraud and favoritism. The new Neighborhood Safety Contract Management Audit Report, which reviews spending from 2020-2025, shows the city is "not providing sufficient contract oversight or managing contracts effectively" in order to properly manage the more than $36 million that has been spent since 2023 on five major violence-prevention programs. The report warns that Minneapolis’ weak contract controls created a heightened risk of fraud and improper payments. Auditors found contractors often submitted invoices with limited supporting documentation, while the city sometimes continued making payments despite missing records or unresolved concerns. The department is also said to have lacked a standardized process for conducting and documenting site visits to verify that contracted services were actually being performed. FINAL WALZ FRAUD REPORT RIPS ‘CULTURE OF TOLERANCE’ AS MINNESOTA TAXPAYERS FACE BILLIONS IN ALLEGED LOSSES Additionally, auditors found the city still needs to improve invoice reviews, preserve contract records, document contractor communications and establish clearer procedures for escalating concerns. "Based on my past reporting on this and other city grant programs, any diligent audit of any city-administered grant programs would produce similar results," Center of the American Experiment policy fellow Bill Glahn told Fox News Digital, pointing to his 2023 reporting on the matter. Glahn’s reporting raised questions about whether Minneapolis’ violence-interrupter program was producing measurable results. In a 2023 analysis, Glahn noted that the city had committed up to $7.5 million to the initiative for 2022–23, with another $13 million included in its budget for 2024–28, while the city had not published substantive evidence demonstrating that the program was reducing violent crime. Glahn also examined the backgrounds and finances of participating organizations, finding that several had annual revenues or staffing levels far below the size of the grants they received. One participant, We Push for Peace, had staffers involved in violent incidents outside St. Paul grocery stores in 2021, including one violence interrupter captured on video beating a homeless man. "The city seems primarily interested in shoveling money out the door to ‘address’ urgent problems," Glahn added. "Little if any care is given to ensuring that the grant recipients are capable of or have a track record of doing the work, are actually doing the work contracted for, or whether that work is resulting in net benefit for city residents and taxpayers." MINNESOTA'S ANTI-ICE AID FUND BECOMES LATEST CASUALTY OF STATE'S EMBARRASSING FRAUD PROBLEM The state has faced heavy criticism in recent years for not conducting enough onsite visits to combat fraud in the Feeding Our Future program along with fraudulent Medicaid programs. "If they would have just gone to the facilities, you know, you hear of the thousands of people being served out of an apartment twice a day, all they would have to do is show up and look at it," Minnesota Republican state Sen. Mark Koran told Fox News Digital in December as the fraud scandal was unfolding. "There was a legislative auditor report that showed that 30 property owners where these businesses claim to operate out of, contacted the Department of Education who manage it, who managed that program, and they told them one, the businesses don't exist in their facilities, so they don't exist, period, and one of them I think was a city park," Koran said. Glahn told Fox News Digital that site visits are "generally helpful" but he suspects that "even a cursory, front-end review of tax records and financial statements would have disqualified many of these vendors from the get-go." "We have not slowed down, there is no sense in which the fraud has been stopped in Minnesota," Glahn told Fox News Digital last month. The audit did not identify a specific instance of fraud, but it warned that Minneapolis’ weak oversight controls created a heightened risk of fraud and improper payments, and many social media users weren't willing to give the state the benefit of the doubt. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Call it what it is," retired Navy intelligence officer Phillip C. Parrish posted on X. "This isn’t a tracking glitch. It’s the same business model that looted child-nutrition money, Medicaid housing, autism therapy, and daycare: stand up a moral emergency, pour cash through politically connected nonprofits, skip site visits and receipts, then scream 'livelihoods' when anyone asks where the money went." Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office for comment. A Minneapolis city spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement, "We appreciate the support of the auditor to make thoughtful, strategic recommendations to improve our department. In fact, the auditor expanded the scope of the report to be more thorough and holistic." The spokesperson added, "The Neighborhood Safety Department has a lot to be proud of. Our work is meaningful, and every day we’re working to make our City safer through innovative safety services, like violence prevention and human trafficking prevention, among others. We’ve taken several steps since the audit report to improve our processes and contract oversight. We are in the business of helping people and improving lives – and that means improving how we do it. It’s that simple."

articles.title: ‘On a scale of 1 to 10, 10’: Trump’s midterm travel schedule underscores GOP troubles
articles.summary: Each trip to play defense robs the GOP of a chance to put Democrats on the back foot in states that are traditionally competitive.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump intends to spend the next 30 days campaigning for Republicans, many of whom are underwater in states the president easily carried two years ago.

Bastions of conservatism — including Alabama, Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — need Trump's star power, and a visit by the president could persuade some of his most die-hard supporters to turn out to the polls. But each trip to play defense in red strongholds robs the GOP of a chance to put Democrats on the back foot in states that are traditionally competitive.

Trump's upcoming travel — including to Alabama, Oklahoma and Ohio this week — puts a focus on what Republican donors and operatives have feared for months: that even a gerrymandered House map and whopping cash advantage won't be enough to save the House or Senate from Democrats.

"The problem is that the fires are everywhere right now," said one GOP donor, who like others in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the party's prospects.

Inside the White House, concern is particularly high over the Senate races in Alaska and Ohio, which the president both won handily in 2024. In Alaska, Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan lost by 8 points in a nonpartisan primary to the Democrat Mary Peltola. Trump is planning to make the trek to Alaska later this month to shore up Sullivan's chances — a significant commitment of time and presidential resources that underscores how dire the situation is for Republicans.

"On a scale of 1 to 10," said a person close to the White House, "10. In Alaska, because of the obvious situation of what happened in the primary, and in Ohio, because [Jon] Husted is proving not to be a compelling candidate."

The White House referred a request for comment to the Republican National Committee. RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre, in a statement, pointed to Republicans' significant financial advantage in the races — coupled with the president's upcoming travel schedule — as two signs of strength heading into the midterms.

"Democrats are struggling to scrounge up two cents to keep key seats in play. Meanwhile, Republicans are deploying our massive war chest, and President Trump is barnstorming the country to drive Republicans to the polls and support our candidates," she said. "Anonymous bed-wetting strategists have no idea what they're talking about and unlike them and the Democrats, we're full steam ahead."

Republicans close to the White House argue trips to ruby red states also have knock-on effects. In addition to boosting the Republican in a gerrymandered House race in Alabama, they expect the president's Friday trip to Mobile, which is part of the Pensacola media market, to also provide a boost in Florida, where Republicans are also facing headwinds. And they expect media from the trip to Durant, Oklahoma, on Thursday to bleed over the border to nearby Dallas.

But campaigning in red states comes at a cost. The president and his team can only be in so many places over the next month, and days spent in Alaska and Iowa are days not spent in Georgia and North Carolina, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.

"They recognize how precious the president's time is," said a second person close to the White House. But "the reality is we have more field to cover than they do. That's just a fact. We are defending more than [Democrats] are."

The president's focus on several states that haven't sent a Democrat to the Senate in decades comes as a series of polls show Trump's favorability reaching record lows. A Wall Street Journal poll released last week found 37% of Americans approve of the job that Trump is doing, the lowest rating for a president heading into a midterm election in Journal polls dating to 1990.

A GOP operative working on races in multiple states said that red states are in "a bad spot for a multitude of reasons," including bad candidate recruitment.

"But [Trump] definitely is the biggest culprit because of how much the trade war has affected the farmers and the Iran war has affected the farmers and rural people," the operative said. "It's his fault."

The average price for a gallon of gas is $4.48, up roughly 10 percent in the last month . Mortgage rates have topped 7%, a two-year high. And the Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates at least one more time this year, raising borrowing costs, in its ongoing effort to tamp down stubborn inflation, which was spurred, in part, by Trump's war with Iran.

"The expanded map reflects the fact that very little has gone right economically for the last 18 months," said one former Trump official. "Now they are scrambling to stop the bleeding."

And it isn't just the president. Vice President JD Vance is headed this week to Texas and Florida, two states the president won by double digits in 2024.

And recently he stumped for Roger Marshall in Kansas and for Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn and Senate candidate Ashley Hinson in Iowa. Hinson, notably, did not attend the event.

"Fucking Vance was in Kansas … not a good sign," said a Texas-based GOP consultant. "We're on defense everywhere. The map's expanding for [Democrats], and there's a limit to what the administration can do."

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. also went to Texas in September for a Head Start program event, joined by GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz and in August, traveled to Iowa to go fishing with "MAHA gubernatorial race superstar" Lahn.

Some Republicans are particularly frustrated that Texas is in play, after Trump intervened in the GOP Senate primary there to support Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. The five most recent polls in the state have Democrat James Talarico up by anywhere from 1 to 6 percentage points over Paxton. MAGA Inc., the super PAC closely aligned with the president, has spent $15 million so far on the Texas Senate race.

But many others expected a tough season as the party in the White House typically struggles during midterm elections.

An RNC official argued GOP donors have known for months that the map would be challenging. It's why the RNC featured Hinson and Sullivan at its quarterly meetings with donors in the run-up to the election, the official said.

"A lot of our donors have been giving to the RNC, giving to the president, for quite some time, and they have kind of weathered the cycles of maps expanding and contracting as we go," the official said. "This is nothing new. This is nothing outside of kind of the noise that they are used to hearing in a typical election cycle."

The Cook Political Report, an independent nonpartisan newsletter that analyzes elections, recently shifted three Senate races and 15 House seats toward Democrats in its ratings. It now lists seven races — those in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas — as toss-ups, with the North Carolina race as "lean Democrat" and the Kansas race"lean Republican."

The best argument for sending Trump to red states is that he can change the electorate, pushing more low-propensity voters who showed up for him in 2024 but don't typically vote in midterm elections to the polls. That might help a Sullivan or Husted pick up enough votes to squeak by.

"You can't take anything for granted when you're the party in power. It's that simple," said another person close to the White House. "Midterm elections are about turnout, and there's nobody better at turning out voters than Donald Trump."

It's a logic some Republican operatives genuinely buy, fearing that his presence in a more traditional battleground could be more detrimental than helpful, considering his low polling numbers. Media from his appearances in red states will, for instance, show up on social media across the country — without risking a candidate having to appear on stage with the president.

"Midterms are base elections," said a fourth person close to the White House. "The president's party wins when his people show up, and there's no better or bigger political engine than a Trump rally."

And RNC officials maintain that Republicans are still competing in the purple states the party had originally planned to focus on. Trump, for instance, was in North Carolina campaigning for former RNC Chair Michael Whatley earlier this month.

"I'll say this: I wish that everybody could see everything at once, but he was in North Carolina two weeks ago. We announced Ohio this Saturday," said a second RNC official. "At the end of all of this, people are going to look at the list … [and] they're going to be like, the president went to places that were very strategically important."

articles.title: Could Trump revoke Ilhan Omar's citizenship for alleged brother marriage? Ex federal prosecutor breaks it down
articles.summary: DHS is conducting a criminal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, but a former federal prosecutor warns of "very high bars" to prove marriage fraud.
articles.body: The Trump administration's recent effort to bring the law down on Rep. Ilhan Omar could go as far as seeking to strip the Minnesota congresswoman of her citizenship for alleged immigration fraud. But a criminal investigation is unlikely to yield the results the president wants, according to a former federal prosecutor. Michael Wildes, an immigration attorney, told Fox News Digital that investigators face a "very high bar" to build a case against Omar after White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is conducting a "criminal" investigation against the progressive "Squad" member. It all stems from claims that Omar married her brother to gain U.S. citizenship, which she has repeatedly denied. President Donald Trump has a longstanding feud with Omar going back to when she was first elected in the middle of his first term, and quickly became one of his most vocal critics in Congress. Trump has repeatedly called for Omar to be sent back to Somalia because of her alleged fraudulent activity. The Trump administration continues to ramp up efforts to denaturalize and deport individuals accused of immigration fraud. And Vice President JD Vance claimed earlier this year that the Department of Justice is investigating Omar for alleged fraud and immigration violations. But questions remain over what a potential prosecution and denaturalization case against the Somali-born lawmaker would require. Wildes said that investigators would need to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Omar knowingly entered her marriage — to a man critics allege is her brother — for the sole purpose of evading U.S. immigration laws. DOJ MOVES TO STRIP CITIZENSHIP FROM 17 PEOPLE ACCUSED OF HIDING DISTURBING CRIMES "In order to establish a successful marriage fraud case, the government would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt… that the defendant knowingly entered into a marriage with the primary purpose to evade immigration laws and get a benefit," Wildes said. Wildes noted that even if Omar and her husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, decided after getting married that their partnership could be a scheme for Elmi to fast pass America’s immigration process, this would not be considered marriage fraud in court. He continued, "Those are very high bars and thresholds that they would have to surmount. The immigration benefit cannot be a byproduct or secondary consideration. This is not deemed to be illegal." If evidence was presented to prove Omar and Elmi committed marriage fraud, the Minnesota Democrat could face up to five years in jail, a maximum fine of $250,000, or both. Wildes also pointed out that there are statutes of limitations that could hinder a potential prosecution and make it more difficult to prosecute Omar for marriage fraud, as that marriage was in 2009. But there is still a pathway for Omar to be denaturalized, which Homan described as a "very serious process" while discussing the investigation into the congresswoman. "The question is: Do they have it factually, and is it the right thing to do?" Wildes said. "The question is whether or not inadvertences were made not purposefully and whether or not it's over the top to then denaturalize somebody," he said. "We're talking about taking away a benefit and then banishing them from the United States." FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME For Omar to be denaturalized, the process would have to be related to allegations that she falsified information when obtaining her own citizenship in 2000. Omar claims she was granted automatic citizenship because she was a minor when her father was naturalized. Congressional records state Omar became a citizen at age 17, but speculation that she was older at the time of her naturalization began after former Minnesota congressional candidate AJ Kern accused Omar’s birth year of being revised on the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library website. This caused allegations to circulate on social media that she was not a minor at the time, which, if ever proven true, could lead to her denaturalization. Even if her father lied in his citizenship paperwork, this could also potentially lead to Omar being stripped of her citizenship. Wildes also explained that the government makes a "case-by-case" decision when it comes to pursuing denaturalization cases. He also pointed out the relevancy of an intentional lie as opposed to a mistake. "If the government were to prosecute for document fraud, we would also want to know whether or not she was represented by counsel, and if there were simple mistakes on her application or inadvertences that may be deemed to be fraudulent," Wildes said. "Whether or not [these] things are truthful, hypothesized, or can be backed up in fact, will play heavily in that prosecution." Homan didn't answer whether the federal government has evidence that Omar committed either marriage or immigration fraud, while also declining to go into detail about what particularly DHS is investigating Omar for. Omar told Fox News Digital just last week that she has not been contacted by DHS or made aware of any ongoing investigation into her marriage or immigration status, saying she isn’t worried about it because "the right wing always had this s--- going." 'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP But Wildes said her being unaware that she is being investigated is not unusual and doesn’t invalidate Homan’s confirmation of a "criminal" investigation against her. "The congresswoman's not being aware doesn't change anything," Wildes said. "There is no obligation for the government to show their hand, and they're going to want to make sure that they have a good prosecution, and they don't give anything up in the interim because of the politics that this presents as well." "I haven't seen anything that I think is worthy of a prosecution," Wildes said. "This is a member of Congress. It may not be your politics, but we have to also make sure that we engage in prosecutions properly and not frivolously." articles.title: Rubio confirms 'foreign actor' involved in UK terror plot
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed a "foreign actor" was behind the thwarted terror plot near RAF Fairford, warning of repercussions tied to Iran.
articles.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that a recent thwarted terror plot near a United Kingdom military base used by the United States involved a "foreign actor," linking the incident to global threats from adversaries such as Iran. "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the U.K. over the weekend is a very serious situation," Rubio told Fox News' "Hannity" on Monday night. "It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor." "I won't get into great detail about that yet." RUBIO QUESTIONS ‘POINT’ OF NATO AFTER ALLIES BLOCKED US FROM USING BASES DURING IRAN CONFLICT Rubio added there would be "repercussions" for threats against U.S. interests. "I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is, we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally," he continued. "We're going to always take that very seriously. There will be repercussions for that, if it ever were to happen or even attempted." Rubio thanked the partners in the U.K. for helping thwart the "very serious threat" of an attack. TRUMP WARNS US WOULD 'DECIMATE AND DESTROY' IRAN OVER ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT "I want to thank the U.K. for their cooperation and their help on it," he said. "There's a lot more news that will come out on this in the days to come. But there's only so much I can say right now at this point about it, other than this was a very serious thing, and it was responded to appropriately." British police declared a major incident at the RAF Fairford base in western England following the arrests early Sunday, and the government held a national emergency meeting. Police, however, released the five on bail Monday but said the investigation was not over, and they were examining whether individuals acting for a foreign state were involved. BRITAIN INTRODUCES SWEEPING NEW POWERS TO TARGET FOREIGN STATE-LINKED GROUPS INCLUDING IRAN'S IRGC President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday that the incident "might be" connected to Iran, which the United States has been at war with since late February, and that he would not have released the suspects on bail. "I wouldn't have done that," he said. A source familiar with the situation told Reuters that three large white vans the men appeared to travel in had not contained viable explosives. TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS The Reuters source said Sunday's police response had not been intelligence-led — an indication that the five were not under direct surveillance — but security had been beefed up at the base, suggesting there was information it was being targeted. The five arrested are all British nationals in their early 20s from London. They were detained in the early hours on Sunday after police were alerted by a local farmer to the three white vans parked near RAF Fairford. Local residents have said security was significantly beefed up at the base in the days leading up to Sunday. The local farmer told reporters that one neighbor, driving past the base on Saturday night, had been ordered by U.S. security personnel to stop and put their hands out of their car. AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11. THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT The farmer, who asked not to be named, called the police after she returned home around 1 a.m. local time and found three large vans parked in the road, one with a fake telephone number on it, and a group of hooded and masked men running away. A large cordon remained around the base Tuesday morning and roadblocks were in place, although local media reports said residents from nearby homes which had been evacuated were returning. Western governments have warned in recent years of the threat of hostile actors from Iran, Russia and elsewhere organizing destabilizing activity or hiring proxies to carry out plots. PUTIN AND IRAN 'NEED EACH OTHER DESPERATELY,' EXPERT SAYS, AS RUSSIA VOICES SUPPORT FOR REGIME Britain raised its national terrorism threat level to its second-highest in April after a series of antisemitic incidents in north London, meaning an attack is considered highly likely. It has also imposed sanctions on individuals and entities linked to Iran, accusing them of involvement in hostile ‌activity including plotting attacks and providing financial services to groups seeking to destabilize Britain and other countries. Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ada Colau, alcaldesa de Barcelona durante ocho años, confirma que ha dejado su piso por no poder llegar a fin de mes: “Con un solo sueldo no podía”
articles.standfirst: El salario actual del alcalde de Barcelona ronda los 100.000 euros anuales brutos
articles.summary: El salario actual del alcalde de Barcelona ronda los 100.000 euros anuales brutos
articles.body: El problema de la vivienda ha copado todos los titulares de los medios españoles. La acampada de la Puerta del Sol y la posterior aprobación de dos decretos por parte del Gobierno, han provocado que el asunto siga en pleno foco de debate. En ‘Café d’idees’ han contado con la presencia de Ada Colau, quien ha revelado una situación personal bastante inesperada. Hay que recordar que fue alcaldesa de Barcelona durante ocho años (2015-2023). El salario por este puesto ronda los 100.000 euros actualmente, en manos de Jaume Collboni. Sin embargo, ella ha reconocido que ha tenido que dejar su casa: “Hasta hace pocos días vivía en un piso de alquiler en el que llevaba más de 15 años, pero con un solo sueldo ya no podía asumir el coste. Así que hemos tenido que ir a compartir vivienda con familiares”. Comenta que su situación personal ha cambiado mucho desde que decidió irse a vivir a aquel inmueble. A pesar de su hipotético buen salario en el pasado, ya no se lo puede permitir: “Aquel piso de alquiler lo cogimos cuando mis hijos eran pequeños. Pero cuando nos separamos, hace cuatro años, tuve que hacerme cargo de un alquiler con un solo salario”. Este, a su juicio, es uno de los principales problemas que tiene actualmente el mercado de la vivienda: “Siempre calcula cuál es la máxima capacidad de pago que existe en la sociedad y da por hecho que, como mínimo, viven dos personas con ingresos en una misma vivienda”. Por eso, cuando las parejas se separan, aparecen los problemas económicos. Si a eso le añades que también hay hijos de por medio, “llega un momento en que ya no puedes asumirlo”, apunta Colau. “Por eso, el piso en el que llevaba más de 15 años he tenido que dejarlo, porque con un solo salario ya no podía hacer frente al coste del alquiler”, reconoce en el espacio de La 2 Cat.

articles.title: 2 Navy aviators eject during landing 'mishap' aboard USS Eisenhower, injuring 4 sailors
articles.summary: Two U.S. Navy aviators ejected while landing on USS Dwight D. Eisenhower off the coast of Virginia, and four sailors aboard were also injured in the mishap.
articles.body: Two U.S. Navy aviators ejected while trying to land their aircraft on USS Dwight D. Eisenhower off the coast of Virginia Monday evening in what the Navy described as a "mishap" that also injured four sailors. The sailors were on board the aircraft carrier at the time. One sailor is being treated for non-life-threatening injuries at a Norfolk-area hospital, the Navy said. The aviators, assigned to Carrier Air Wing 3, were successfully brought back to the ship by search and rescue personnel. They are being evaluated by medical personnel, the Navy said. ONE CREW MEMBER MISSING AFTER US NAVY HELICOPTER MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING IN ARABIAN SEA The Navy did not reveal which type of two-seater plane was involved in the accident. It also did not specify what happened to the plane or what could have happened to cause the accident. The Navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. USS Dwight D. Eisenhower, a nuclear-powered Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, entered service in 1977. The incident follows several recent mishaps in which military aviators had to eject. PILOT EJECTS AS F-35 CRASHES AT MCAS MIRAMAR, SPARKING FIRE In May, four Navy crew members ejected safely after two EA-18G Growlers collided during an aerial demonstration at Mountain Home Air Force Base in Idaho. Both aircraft, worth about $67 million apiece, crashed after they collided. Former TOPGUN pilot Matthew "Whiz" Buckley told Fox News Digital last month how ejecting from an aircraft traveling at high speed can lead to lifelong injuries, when the pilot is lucky enough to survive. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Buckley said some people he knew who had to eject suffered spinal injuries that left them several inches shorter. "When you pull that handle, you have two choices: die or maybe live. And I said, 'maybe live' because it's incredibly violent," Buckley said. "Most folks don't even remember the ejection. They remember pulling the handle and then waking up in their parachute."

articles.title: Jack Smith's Trump probe swept up Fox News, other media communications as investigation went beyond lawmakers
articles.summary: Jack Smith's investigators obtained records containing communications between nearly 50 journalists and government officials during the Trump probe.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Former special counsel Jack Smith's investigators obtained records containing communications between nearly 50 journalists and Trump administration officials — including Fox News personnel — after subpoenaing text-message records associated with dozens of White House phones during the federal election investigation of President Donald Trump, Fox News Digital has learned ahead of Tuesday's Senate Judiciary Committee hearing. Previous congressional disclosures showed investigators obtained records involving members of Congress. The latest records reveal the production also included communications between government officials and journalists working for some of the country's largest news organizations. The communications appeared in records produced by the National Archives in response to a subpoena seeking material associated with 87 White House phones from Trump's first administration, according to a spokesperson for Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, citing whistleblower disclosures made to the chairman. "What will the partisan media say about this disgraceful government overreach? This wasn’t a normal prosecution by any means," Grassley challenged in comments to Fox News Digital on Tuesday, as critics have highlighted the lack of concern or coverage given to Smith’s probe by legacy media. EXPLOSIVE NEW REPORT PUTS JACK SMITH BACK IN HOT SEAT AS JIM JORDAN ALLEGES HE TRIED TO 'SWAY' 2024 ELECTION One organization identified Tuesday as having been swept up in the probe was the Media Research Center. Its president, David Bozell, announced in 2025 that "not one single broadcast network aired one solitary second" about Smith’s alleged spying on conservative organizations and senators following a tranche of public disclosures. Fox News is among the organizations whose journalists appear in the records, along with CNN, CBS News — including its newsmagazine "60 Minutes" — NBC News and CNBC. The records also include communications involving journalists from the Wall Street Journal, Washington Post, Bloomberg, Los Angeles Times, New York Magazine, Reuters, the Associated Press and NPR, as well as The Federalist and Washington Times. READ THE LIST: 44 LAWMAKERS SWEPT INTO JACK SMITH TEXT SWEEP AS HIS LEGAL RECKONING GROWS The nationally syndicated "The Mark Levin Show," hosted by Fox News host and former Reagan Justice Department chief of staff Mark Levin, also appears in the records. The records stem from a June 2, 2023, subpoena issued by Smith’s office to the National Archives seeking text messages from phones associated with numerous officials who served in the first Trump White House. JACK SMITH HIT WITH CRIMINAL REFERRAL AS GOP MOVES TESTIMONY FIGHT TOWARD PROSECUTION The Archives produced responsive records on Aug. 21, 2023, according to documents previously disclosed through congressional oversight by Grassley and Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., of Arctic Frost. Grassley and Johnson pressed the Justice Department and FBI in May for information about how potentially privileged material in that production was screened before investigators could review it. An Aug. 21, 2023 email from assistant special counsel Thomas Windom instructed members of Smith’s team, including prosecutors and FBI personnel, to download documents associated with text messages from the White House phones. "We are writing to determine what procedures and protocols, if any, Smith and his team used to filter privileged or potentially privileged materials from being impermissibly accessed, reviewed and/or used," Grassley and Johnson wrote. The senators requested DOJ’s filtering protocols and the names of officials assigned to review material for privilege before it reached investigators. The committee has identified the individual journalists whose communications appear in the records but does not plan to release their names because of privacy concerns, a Grassley spokesperson told Fox News Digital. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The disclosure broadens questions surrounding Smith’s handling of the White House records ahead of Tuesday’s Senate hearing, including what safeguards governed investigators’ access to communications involving lawmakers, journalists and other third parties. The Judiciary Committee is expected to examine Smith’s investigative practices and the broader scope of Arctic Frost. Grassley also pressed Smith about another revelation from the senator's recent investigation into the former special counsel's probe. The Iowa Republican asked whether Smith's operation obtained donor data, including the financial and personal information of rank-and-file civilians who gave even small sums to political candidates. Smith acknowledged the claim, saying he could not recite "every subpoena we issued" but that the purpose was "to conduct a criminal investigation of one of the most serious crimes that's ever happened in our nation's history," referring to the allegations against Trump. "Indeed, you did," Grassley fumed in reply, citing disclosures to his office that Smith "obtained at least 4,782 donor[s'] checks. Many of those checks were $5 to $10. The list includes checks from constituents in every state of every single member of this committee, both Republicans and Democrats. It included 42 checks from Iowans who dared to donate money to Republicans," he said. Grassley argued there was "no legitimate basis" for what he described as a violation of donors' privacy. articles.title: Inside Operation Blackout: Patel reveals global scam ‘cities’ targeting your parents’ life savings
articles.summary: FBI Director Kash Patel says Operation Blackout has seized roughly $17 billion tied to scam compounds targeting senior citizens across the globe.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: FBI Director Kash Patel says the bureau is expanding its global hunt for sprawling scam compounds that prey heavily on Americans, telling Fox News Digital that Operation Blackout has seized roughly $17 billion tied to the schemes. "At 71 years old, I'm old enough to know that people my age are certainly often targeted because of our unfamiliarity with certain new technologies. Thanks so much for looking out for us," one victim told the FBI. "I watched my grandmother lose her life savings to scammers and I would love to see them all be put away," said another victim. Operation Blackout is the FBI’s global campaign to identify, disrupt and dismantle foreign scam compounds targeting Americans, combining overseas raids and asset seizures with efforts to cut off the networks’ communications, rescue trafficked workers and return stolen money to victims. FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS Patel said the FBI-led initiative is targeting criminal syndicates operating massive scam compounds across Southeast Asia and the Middle East, where trafficked workers are forced to carry out fraud schemes against victims thousands of miles away. "Unfortunately, the majority of the targets are senior citizens in America," Patel told Fox News Digital, pointing to schemes carried out through social media, phone calls, text messages and Telegram. "Our initiative, Operation Blackout, is to prevent, disrupt, and dismantle," Patel added. FBI SEIZES RECORD-SETTING $8 BILLION IN CRYPTOCURRENCY AMID INTERCONTINENTAL 'SCAM COMPOUND' CRACKDOWN In one common version of the scheme, criminals cultivate an online friendship or relationship with a victim before steering them toward a fraudulent cryptocurrency investment platform. Victims may initially believe their investments are generating significant returns, only to discover they cannot withdraw their money. "These are towns, these are cities," Patel said of the scam compounds targeted by the operation. "These are actual villages with structures where they force people into forced labor." An August operation at Cambodia’s roughly 200-acre O’Smach Resort scam compound involved searches of 28 buildings over three days and resulted in the seizure of 113 hard drives, 15 computers and 35 boxes of evidence, according to the FBI. The bureau is also trying to stop Americans from becoming victims before their money ever reaches the scammers. SCAMMERS ARE COMING FOR YOUR MONEY. HERE’S THE ONE THING YOU MUST NEVER DO Under Operation Level Up, its domestic prevention component working with U.S. Secret Service, the FBI proactively identifies and contacts potential victims of cryptocurrency investment scams. The bureau says it has notified 10,406 victims and prevented an estimated $660 million in losses, while seizing or freezing another $122 million in cryptocurrency. The FBI said 77% of the people it contacted did not know they were being scammed. The bureau has also referred 99 victims for suicide intervention, seized 584 scam websites and sent 7,670 scam accounts to private-sector companies for action. THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET In September, a DOJ Scam Center Strike Force team that included FBI Honolulu personnel helped authorities in Madagascar take down 13 scam centers operated by Chinese organized crime syndicates and process more than 3,200 electronic devices. Patel said the geographic shift is part of a broader migration by the criminal networks. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "That’s why you’re seeing the migration of these scam compounds to central and sub-Saharan Africa, which is where we are already pre-positioned to take them off," Patel said.

articles.title: Republicans fear they ‘haven’t done a damn thing’ to lower prices ahead of midterm reckoning
articles.summary: Senate Republicans spent weeks passing the Protect College Sports Act while Sen. Josh Hawley and others warn affordability concerns are being ignored.
articles.body: The key focus of this election, like many before it, is the economy, but the Senate has spent its waning weeks in Washington focusing on something else: college sports. And that has proven a sticking point for some Republicans who are eager to maintain power in the upper chamber and worried that they aren’t meeting the moment to address voters’ concerns over the cost-of-living. "I'm just hoping that this will be the best bill ever passed by the United States Senate considering the ungodly amount of time we've spent on it," Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told Fox News Digital. "So maybe this will be the most perfect and pristine piece of legislation ever," he quipped. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS "There's a lot of things we could be doing and should be doing," the senator added. "So I hope we'll do those before we leave. We'll see." Hawley rattled off those issues that he hoped lawmakers would tackle that all ended in one word, costs — be it for fuel, prescription drugs, health care or the financial burden of the artificial intelligence boom. The Senate is expected to leave the nation’s capital on Wednesday to hit the campaign trail for the homestretch of the fast-approaching midterm elections. But from the summer of 2025 to now, with several shutdowns and partisan fights in between, the sting on voters’ wallets, to some concerned Republicans, has become an afterthought. Still, Republicans are quick to tout their accomplishments from last year, notably the "big, beautiful bill," as their signature achievement to tackle the growing issue of affordability in the country — it was a predominant pitch during the midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month, and can be heard increasingly in the halls of the Senate as Nov. 3 nears. SENATE MOVES TO REIN IN COLLEGE SPORTS 'WILD WEST' WITH SWEEPING NEW RULES FOR PLAYERS, SCHOOLS The concern over inaction in the recent weeks and months has intensified as the main business in the Senate has been devoted to passing the Protect College Sports Act from Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, which cruised through the upper chamber late Monday night. "We've been spending all week on trying to make the football coaches happy," Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said. "I'm voting for the bill, but I can assure that moms and dads out there across America, when they lie down to sleep at night … they're not worried about the football coaches." Kennedy said that he and others have been pressuring Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., to take another shot at reconciliation tailored exclusively toward affordability issues, or at the very least to put a bill that would shield consumers from increasing electricity costs as part of the AI boom. "Because we haven't done a damn thing," Kennedy said. "And it's biting us in the ass right now." ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER Thune did tee up what will likely be the Senate’s last attempt at dealing with affordability for a vote this week on a bill that would require AI companies to bear the brunt of rising utility costs from data centers. That bill, from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is expected to be blocked by Democrats, however, who aren’t eager to give Republicans or Trump a victory — especially so close to the midterm elections. But for some Republicans, it’s too little too late when it comes to actually trying to address voters’ worries. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., recalled a story when he won the North Carolina House and became speaker. He ran to fix the economy, and once he won the power to do so, he and Republicans in the state would have to own the issue, regardless of the previous administration’s actions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "That's how you actually show some leadership and get it done. You can't rationalize that we're here because of a problem caused by the prior administration," Tillis told Fox News Digital. "That's how we got elected. But you gotta fix it if you promise to. And that's what we have to work on. I just think rationalizing away, that's just not good politics." Still, Republicans are asking for a second chance this fall, specifically Vice President JD Vance, who earlier this month asked voters to "give us another chance." When asked about Vance’s plea, Tillis said, "You know what? If it works, it'll be a first."

articles.title: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
articles.summary: The US president continues to push back on calls to establish guardrails around artificial intelligence, arguing it will stifle growth.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.

Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.

Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.

The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.

During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US is "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and does not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.

"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."

Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remains steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.

"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".

Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder AI governance.

Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.

A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.

A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.

The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

articles.title: Drug cartel kingpin among targets in sweeping Trump crackdown on alleged Mexican corruption network
articles.summary: The Sinaloa Cartel's Los Mayos faction faces sweeping Treasury sanctions targeting Mayito Flaco, a fugitive born in Anaheim accused of ordering hits.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration is seeking to disrupt with a sweeping set of sanctions a sprawling Sinaloa Cartel network accused of corrupting Mexican officials just across the U.S. border. Los Mayos, a powerful faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, and its U.S.-born leader are accused of funneling fentanyl and drug money through California and hiring hitmen to kill rivals on American soil. The Treasury Department, according to material exclusively obtained by Fox News Digital ahead of their public release on Tuesday, will sanction 21 individuals and 25 entities in a crackdown against Los Mayos and their alleged illegal activity within U.S. borders. The targets of the sanctions include Ismael Zambada Sicairos, known as "Mayito Flaco," a dual U.S.-Mexican citizen born in Anaheim, California, whom Treasury describes as the "undisputed head" of Los Mayos. MEXICAN GOVERNOR FACING US DRUG CHARGES SEEKS LEAVE JUST ONE DAY AFTER RETURNING TO OFFICE The action lays out how one of Mexico’s most powerful cartel factions allegedly maintains its grip on two critical trafficking corridors along the U.S. border — through political and police corruption, money laundering and violence that Treasury says has extended into Southern California. It also exposes what Treasury describes as deep cartel penetration of government and law enforcement in Baja California, the Mexican state bordering California. Treasury says Sinaloa-linked "narco-corruption has reached the highest levels" of the state government, alleging that the ex-husband of Gov. Marina del Pilar Ávila Olmeda used his political influence to protect cartel operations and that a former Mexicali public security chief accepted bribes to allow the cartel to exert control over municipal police. The allegations shed new light on a controversy that erupted last year when the U.S. revoked the visas of both Ávila and her then-husband, Carlos Torres Torres. Treasury now says the State Department revoked Torres’ visa in May 2025 because of his "cartel affiliation and work on behalf of the Sinaloa Cartel." U.S. officials had not publicly disclosed why Ávila’s visa was revoked. The State Department revoked Torres’ U.S. visa in May 2025 over what Treasury now describes as his "cartel affiliation and work on behalf of the Sinaloa Cartel." Ávila’s U.S. visa was also revoked around the same time, though U.S. officials did not publicly disclose a reason for the action against her. POTENTIAL SECURITY THREAT PROMPTS US TRAVEL SUSPENSION FOR BORDER CITY ON ALERT Treasury also alleges the cartel’s reach extended directly into California. Lorenzo Castillo Maldonado, an associate in Mayito Flaco’s network, allegedly hired hitmen on the cartel leader’s orders to kill rival cartel members in Southern California. Another part of the network allegedly worked with complicit Southern California money exchanges to collect bulk cash from U.S. drug sales and move the proceeds back to Mexico. The sanctions are aimed in part at disrupting Los Mayos’ grip on the Tijuana and Mexicali "plazas," strategic corridors Treasury says the cartel uses to move fentanyl and other narcotics into the U.S. "Today’s action underscores that no cartel kingpin, corrupt Mexican government official, or financial facilitator is beyond the reach of Treasury’s authorities," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. "Our message is clear: the Trump Administration will identify and disrupt any cartel actor who threatens our security or the integrity of our financial system." The designations effectively cut the targets off from the U.S. financial system, blocking property and assets under U.S. jurisdiction and generally barring Americans from doing business with them. Foreign financial institutions that knowingly facilitate significant transactions for sanctioned individuals could also face U.S. sanctions. At the center of Tuesday’s action is Mayito Flaco, who Treasury says has emerged as the undisputed leader of Los Mayos following the July 2024 arrest of his father, longtime Sinaloa Cartel kingpin Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada Garcia. SINALOA CARTEL BOSS 'EL MAYO' SENTENCED TO LIFE, ORDERED TO PAY $15B IN DRUG TRAFFICKING PROFITS El Mayo’s arrest set off a violent struggle between Los Mayos and Los Chapitos, the Sinaloa faction led by sons of Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman. Treasury says the two factions remain locked in a costly internal war that has forced both sides to rebuild their leadership and alliances. Mayito Flaco, 44, was born in Anaheim in 1982 and later filed a U.S. name change to Fernando Sicairos Aispuro, according to Treasury. He was federally indicted in California in 2014 on drug trafficking and money laundering charges and remains a fugitive in Mexico. Treasury says he now commands Los Mayos’ drug trafficking, murder, extortion, corruption and kidnapping operations. The sanctions also target Torres’ brother, Luis Alfonso Torres Torres, whom Treasury accuses of collecting bribes and laundering illicit funds through companies and political campaigns. Treasury alleges Mendivil accepted bribes from Los Rusos leader Juan Jose Ponce Felix, known as "El Ruso," in exchange for allowing the cartel to exert control over municipal police, facilitate drug trafficking and carry out enforcement operations.
